messages.s_a2ce139a6c71afea3a11ed2aeaea2aa22aba52: I could freeze after each step without leaning.
messages.s_15c15d401fb5852fd74d568b85a0cb669dd76a: My trailing foot restored, rather than erased, stance width.
messages.s_bc8d27dc2e00deae4543004b9f8b6fdd35c6c8: I can name the initiating foot for each side and stop without crossing.
messages.s_7efdf18fa1396b947df0971aff1a6eb3aa71b4: Use two-inch side shifts or a supported standing position when the full step is difficult.
messages.s_8cdc4af20d9701044cc6a0242eb0680c93bbdf: Stop if the knees or ankles hurt or you cannot keep the path clear.

messages.s_939e70419cb434bc00055c39a8ffb970e404cd: Change both distance and side without tangling the feet.

messages.s_e9ccc3f7ac6436047d94557608ff990e433fe9: Do not cross the feet when reaching a corner. Reduce the diagonal distance and wait for the second foot to restore the base.
messages.s_1b00afad5b289f05b1ec96633d00b2c868501b:
Draw a small X mentally and travel one arm-length along each ray, returning to the centre between rays.

Short focused practice: Try the two front rays of a small X first, then the two back rays after a rest. Stop at the centre on every return and name the next direction beforehand. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose the small X rays in a different order while keeping the return to the centre.

messages.s_4b42409381465d3e6342efab85e963a6f8f8de: Each trip ended in the same stance width.
messages.s_176ad0f9bdc035b1e9bb9f5cdfb15aecbfd9af: I could name which foot started each direction.
messages.s_bd466d5c4370dbd677ee5c738eb77a4010bea0: I can choose the first foot toward each small corner and return to a comfortable base at the centre.
messages.s_4fa97ef497c2184c922891b5276da1b2db0c50: Shrink the X or trace it with weight shifts only; keep a stable reference point nearby.
messages.s_e23bd01b970f59f7450dbbc332052c7e9d7118: Stop if turning a corner brings dizziness or unexpected joint pain.
messages.s_d60804dfaf8226252bb411f5dad379d5ed29c7: Original overhead X diagram plus front three-quarter performer view, pausing after each diagonal.
messages.s_8e61cb34f7c18da6c13ba78ac35260f16f958b: Reorient the stance without twisting a planted knee.
messages.s_4a1c6bf4be6a6d689781f78f6acb3391fbddfb: Move the rear foot in a small arc while the lead foot turns comfortably on the ball; let hips and shoulders face the new direction together.
messages.s_271c4aa6d8948641949031e5c33b1ea21b9115: Make only a modest turn, stop, and rebuild the guard. A pivot is an exit to a new line, not a spin for speed.
messages.s_d09a18bae4d4c87118be6569ffc9efee638835: Do not twist the knee over a fixed lead foot or force a large turn. Reduce the angle and step the lead foot as well if needed.
messages.s_f7cc7ac95566be07961601d2dbdfdfbbcd5133:
Make three small turns each way with a full reset and a pause after each.

messages.s_416185d58b92780892b27acc64d53276f7efa1: My knee followed the foot rather than twisting under it.

messages.s_2545c686636bbd9ce89935276bf2d7d4f6bddd: Use an even smaller arc or step the lead foot to turn if pivoting on one foot is uncomfortable.
messages.s_2a9cf8124e7ba3581761b2449a18b838878125: Stop with knee, ankle or hip pain, or if the surface grips the foot and forces twisting.

messages.s_c9db6a4b2729aac20b2aee7ac9f7d717d37a0d: Step back or diagonally out before resetting. Keep the feet underneath you on entry and exit.
messages.s_43ec096f660b03fb71ef95e2e2fc3d17c5f290: Reaching an imagined point by bending at the waist changes the distance drill. Move the point closer or enter with a small step; strike no real object.

Repeat five entry-pause-exit cycles, alternating the exit direction; the hands stay in guard.

Short focused practice: In the five entry-stop-exit cycles, try back exits in the first two and small diagonal exits in the next two; choose the comfortable option for the last. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

messages.s_ba7d9542743beb164da21e1ca274df3af8c1ea: I can enter without falling forward to reach and recover a ready base on exit.
messages.s_1e061a6629b149d81cef8481d49c7e96b190f9: Use a shorter entry or mark a closer imagined spot if balance or reach is limited.
messages.s_01cba08093b779a7b4678b4ed325f9b8e98e50: Stop if you begin lunging into furniture or pain changes how you step.
messages.s_199a9747843c14dd61f1abaa2213f1a00491d3: Original side-on wide frame shows imagined target line, step-in pause and diagonal exit; no impact effect.
messages.s_301772e95da5381612905a6ef113d57d096c07: Learn the lead and rear straight line slowly, with a complete return to guard after each action.
messages.s_efbd4805ae402bd845fa46573abdd977808f75: Extend the lead hand on a direct path while the rear hand stays ready.
messages.s_fb2de5a69e63d52e11d13d436c97f08f733d02: Begin in guard. Let the lead hand travel toward an imagined eye-level point, without winding it behind the shoulder first.
messages.s_f75e6071fa9206987c7ff11036589ec44d5834: Keep the rear hand near the cheek and the head over the feet. Reach within your comfortable range; do not lock or snap the elbow.
messages.s_5247ef21a5950ce1c1e1e7fef58f5bf15456bb: Do not snap-lock the elbow or pull the hand back first for a jab. Use a small straight path from comfortable guard, shorten the reach and return along it.
messages.s_ebe876bb4406ef467cda460d3493cd880aa8f0:
Perform six slow lead-hand reaches to one imagined point, fully pausing in guard between them.

Short focused practice: Choose two short groups of three slow lead-hand reaches, stopping in full guard after each. Focus on the straight path in one group and rear-hand readiness in the other. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose the jab after a small entry, establishing the base and guard first.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit A relaxed guard; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_6c22a05c38dc0aed33c7617cb8186a0f39ad15: The lead hand took a direct path rather than a wide arc.
messages.s_99f65117b2ea03432e4c63c39e7f8176223d0f: The rear hand stayed available while the lead hand moved.
messages.s_a71a9efe974ad4a816e11590c042ca3895104d: I can rehearse a comfortable lead-hand straight path and return without moving the rear hand away.
messages.s_3ecbe7bafe64619ee540a1d6ec44059367c0f3: Shorten the reach and reduce repetitions if the shoulder or elbow is uncomfortable; do not force full extension.
messages.s_b40c3860981bc8a77641f8b0f432949e0f2887: Stop if the wrist, elbow or shoulder hurts sharply or if balance moves beyond the lead foot.
messages.s_64fcf135d38f5643105e1c2aebb36026cc4ceb: Original three-quarter and side views show lead-hand path and rear-hand guard; no speed or force number.
messages.s_5fd644646f20ad60a3e2a23736640a732b7626: Finish a jab by bringing the lead hand back to guard before moving again.
messages.s_89ea9fe0cbcbbc5fd7730a21c11e872738b109: Reach to the same imagined point as before. Reverse the path with the elbow and hand returning together; avoid letting the hand hang low on the way back.
messages.s_9848c203c6cd16756aeabb90a2b0f7154fe8e1: Pause with both hands visible in your own field of view. One reach plus return is a whole repetition.
messages.s_6cdd0e12700e2792beaddf8104a46ed801481e: Do not return the jab by looping the hand downwards. Use a short path and notice that it reaches the starting place before the next repetition.
messages.s_63ce22900a0d919f4dd342c317ac1f8451d3cb:
Do two sets of five slow jabs. On each return say 'home' quietly before the next one.

Short focused practice: Say home after each return in the first of the existing two five-repetition groups; reduce the cue in the second and start the next jab from a ready hand. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Add a small back exit after the single jab's return.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit The lead-hand jab; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_23d0a0b193c5998643bef941625e496b57148c: I waited for the hand to return before the next reach.
messages.s_2b86ba3811d3da6ea70234c0f06a682435a2d7: My chin and balance did not follow the fist forward.
messages.s_1faad5232fb9f2d8c96946ca267d7b75826c74: I do not start the next repetition before the jab returns and can practise recovery separately.
messages.s_442f231e59f6570e47e11dfd58aacdfbc6d863: Use fewer repetitions and a partial reach; a clean return matters more than reaching far.
messages.s_a527330d286e3219ca9c54447231355b17e973: Stop when return quality breaks down or any upper-limb pain appears.
messages.s_ff1706fc90956155966e8db27f31e4bdf40a51: Original split-screen: outbound and return paths with a freeze on the recovered guard, not a punch counter.
messages.s_02e2dd32379ca056e6dd73d1551e2330701a6e: Repeat the lead straight without losing the rear-hand guard or foot spacing.
messages.s_80d59cd4eadac5f2f1a5efa404dfad11ce5bad: Send one small jab, let it return, then send a second. The second begins from guard, not from a hand left in midair.
messages.s_63372e95d56ae5ab403d9ea6850785dc85aedf: Keep the same imagined target and an easy rhythm. Do not speed up until both returns are complete.
messages.s_274572258a811ac0bc66737745f3bef2fae2ae: Do not shorten the first return to rush the second jab. Count two separate jabs and two separate returns, then connect them comfortably.
messages.s_ddfa611487b6fa0397c30a79f1ff205f44a5cf:
Perform five double-jab pairs with a full stance reset between pairs.

Short focused practice: Pause through jab-return-jab-return for the first two of the existing five pairs; in the remaining pairs focus only on starting the second jab from guard. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a slow small side exit after the double jab without skipping either return.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Return to your base; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_f188b37e78fb6247c183a6864986772d8e9f01: I could distinguish two separate starts from guard.
messages.s_48f2dfa2591ee8cc07082ec07f71d168f4422f: The rear hand did not follow the jabs downward.
messages.s_3739db6d326b6f4a68db5061c3d33a920cf429: I can distinguish both jab returns and finish the pair in the same base.
messages.s_b05e8f8540b7c815518899463c031b38764c3a: Practise one jab at a time until the return is clear; a smaller reach is acceptable.
messages.s_848e898e7d3f3d54d3d3a5f44ed1ec43a016fc: Stop when the pair becomes a rushed arm flail or balance is lost.
messages.s_7195e545e74a82505e0cc3904d49f84a23444d: Original front three-quarter shot labels start, return, start, return; show rear hand in every frame.
messages.s_51d2946cf5a4a8f40e1f3ed5c78bc86fd478d4: Coordinate the rear hand with a comfortable turn through the base.
messages.s_436171e94979ce7064429a66bc313585358bfb: From guard, allow the rear foot, hip and shoulder to turn as the rear hand travels on a straight imagined line. Keep the lead hand ready.
messages.s_0368b16aa3b5cc8134705e2c9dc2afd6de9278: Do not force a large twist or chase reach by leaning. The whole body stops in a base from which the hand can return.
messages.s_40e641f89699f29f89b429e2f1343719729842: Do not throw the head beyond the base while extending the rear straight. Keep the comfortable foot-and-torso turn small, leave the lead hand ready and shorten the reach.
messages.s_9242f14aa2c4609c63fdedac7ec12b521ace20:
Make six slow rear-hand straights, checking the lead guard and foot position after each.

Short focused practice: In three of the existing six slow repetitions focus only on the small direction change, and in three on lead-hand readiness. Rebuild the base after each. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Rehearse the rear-straight path separately after a small forward step without increasing reach.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Find your stance; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_8ac689100ed39c83d991bfb92be1daa34b0e24: The turn felt comfortable through foot, hip and shoulder, not forced in one joint.
messages.s_ba602ec2bfb9b031413c2de21bacfccb264d66: The lead hand stayed near guard.
messages.s_af289ad415c2a56ff8f3b8719ccc34f6100121: I can rehearse a comfortable rear-straight path, keep the lead hand ready and return to my base.
messages.s_f1dbdc07714c9320b558be2bd383b2c703c801: Use a small torso turn or a shorter reach; ask a qualified coach about individual movement limits.
messages.s_038184c7444a902010f13c762341579295b6b6: Stop for back, hip, knee, shoulder or wrist pain, especially during the turn.
messages.s_286191ed5a2ee35564ee216da6ff2c297aa89e: Original rear-side three-quarter view and foot inset show comfortable whole-body turn, no fixed angle target.
messages.s_a616cc821eb87a380c2d3f68230e2677f62d1b: Return the rear hand and base together before another action.
messages.s_35cc99dd83bab84bd02a1bdd2d7b2b86f834a4: After a slow rear straight, bring the rear hand to the cheek as the turning foot and hip settle back into stance.
messages.s_27ec7f8f23ebbe22be0f06fc09c88d552aa754: Avoid leaving the rear shoulder ahead or the hand low. Pause after every return and check both hands and feet.
messages.s_7b62132a837e5e54842ad34e49d5ac0c5d5511: Do not leave the torso turned and the hand low after the rear straight. Rehearse the hand's return and the feet's comfortable base recovery separately and slowly.
messages.s_d32d0176e5ced4365b69743d09db03d51f08ea:
Alternate one rear straight and a three-breath guard pause for five repetitions.

Short focused practice: Practise only the reduced recovery portion in the first two of the existing five repetitions, then connect extend-return-stop in the remainder. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a small back exit rather than moving forward after the rear recovery.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Return to your base; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_02e1b1214eeee724d2116477090c68d977187f: The rear hand arrived home before I began again.
messages.s_26dbf1f941087b311c6a3fa11fb1bcc6a18082: My stance after the punch matched the stance before it.
messages.s_99db012b2bdaa94a3f056362948c38aded4e56: I wait for the rear hand and base to return before another movement and can describe recovery deliberately.
messages.s_894a5df7e3c52a4c0d738917621cb5db43d4bf: Use a shorter rear-hand path and more time to settle if coordination is hard.
messages.s_398365aedf6cfa2ceec5a09d98d0ea73c242af: Stop if repeated turning causes discomfort or dizziness.
messages.s_c6ce900e0354681f4d67cf8c994ae46711b26b: Original side-on sequence includes start, extension, hand return and feet reset as four distinct frames.
messages.s_e5c2730707d5d6c6cad3c7c51bb01aa329388a: Link one lead straight and one rear straight while preserving the guard between them.
messages.s_f74e67e7e56e5d0a47c1c189d57ed0fbba1d38: Send a jab and start its return. Then turn into the rear straight while the lead hand comes home; do not send both hands away together.
messages.s_e0edf7c8ef922dc9210512164f58bfff674198: Finish in the original stance with both hands ready. Make each pair slow enough to identify its two parts.
messages.s_8a5636eebac7c4bdb724df41dec388bc63ac0f: Do not leave both hands forward in the one-two. Learn slowly with separate returns first; keep the lead hand's return path as the rear straight begins in the linked version.
messages.s_8fb69891ca93d84cd7e854f3c49e193dcfd043:
Do six slow one-two pairs with a full pause after each pair; imagine a target, never a person.

Short focused practice: Pause through jab-return-rear straight-return for the first two pairs. In the next two shorten only the connecting pause comfortably and finish in the full base. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a familiar back or side exit yourself after the one-two.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit The jab comes home; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_b75e7bc75704c4336f2c0bb832cf7948a2a546: The lead hand was returning as the rear hand departed.
messages.s_2183e0e879d1bc1c8d885617760f5faa1ad33d: I ended in a stance I could step from.
messages.s_464be967d8815fd52bef3afb50d016f23150ff: I can distinguish the two straight paths and bring both hands to readiness at the pair's end.
messages.s_7d1c7e4766821841f6d0d39c2c6fbf508d7fda: Separate the pair with an extra guard pause or return to single punches if timing becomes tangled.
messages.s_0b00eb00bfc52e1fb4b0d35484929c57ad6824: Stop if you lose balance or upper-limb pain appears while linking the two actions.
messages.s_8c4a789fe62f23b2f869ac2890ed694ecfa4c9: Original wide three-quarter demonstration with two distinct numbered phases and a visible final reset; no combination score.
messages.s_0ee6b83e69972aad178e83e40d08db2d2f642e: Rehearse planned exits and guard movements without claiming a real attack or reaction time.
messages.s_d2b65bd721f2dbd85a60c2933c6b3a66162542: Leave an imagined attack line by stepping to a stable position.
messages.s_e37f6371693f64605847bc73252694b95cef9c: Mark an imagined line from in front of you. Take one small backward step, recover the trailing foot, then stop in guard.
messages.s_6c20d7be2116d6cb6eec4b46be2d3c322e0a85: Repeat with a diagonal exit. These are rehearsed directions, not a tested response to an opponent.
messages.s_63fa7a551eaaf1290bc12b8f960fc902cd7c18: Do not treat a planned back step as proof of avoiding a real attack. Rehearse only space and base management here and ask no partner to attack.
messages.s_97fe300ed0ff6cccad1386bf9db7e9b5c9c285:
Alternate five backward and five diagonal planned exits, resetting the feet and guard each time.

Short focused practice: Pause through the first two back and first two diagonal exits, then choose a sequence of the two familiar exits and rebuild guard after each. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Swap the back and diagonal exit order without increasing an imagined attack's speed.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Enter and leave range; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_9609e16f9b8afb7695cc4c561773c108e82f5f: I finished each exit balanced and able to move again.
messages.s_5f91544c310858b2edd5adcbe1aba4c5e95787: I did not call this a measured defensive reflex.
messages.s_b341d06dd7e2106281caeb0b0920c15685898a: I can choose two planned exit paths and understand that this rehearsal is not a reaction to a real attack.
messages.s_e882e3776d86cbe84ffd76b84b0d06e5f7fc21: Use shorter exits or a supported weight shift when space or balance is limited.
messages.s_862e977cb52376d685ad3cd91452b5e990fb2b: Stop if an exit approaches an obstacle or makes you stumble.
messages.s_25bf0beaa45e8b504729e2a9dbb94b14d7709b: Original overhead line and two exit arrows; no incoming human punch or reflex timer.
messages.s_02d08df4fb44fe57867d67c20312b54e7289fc: Bring the hands close without losing sight or collapsing the stance.
messages.s_1dec751f922e57f5328b954876ef93e44cf724: From relaxed guard, bring both hands a little closer to the temples and let elbows settle comfortably toward the body.
messages.s_9f29d70a4ffb330821907b08e05174fde07268: Take one small step out, then return to ordinary guard. Avoid squeezing so hard that shoulders rise and breathing stops.
messages.s_c9321a08e6c325e42bd21773d89beca06583a1: Do not build a cover by closing the eyes or squeezing the shoulders hard. Keep the hands comfortably compact, the gaze open and reset with a small step.
messages.s_47cb784340969b2fe94b897d55684f48235c66:
Practise six cover-step-reset cycles slowly, alternating exit sides.

Short focused practice: Focus only on comfortable vision in two cover-step-return cycles, then only on the foot base in the next two. Lower the hands to rest. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose another small exit direction after the cover and rebuild the base.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit A relaxed guard; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_73a2567b70e4d68c40afd18523b07d0f47f329: I could still see the imagined line ahead.
messages.s_8df359bd066959f3161774c79588e083c02fbc: My shoulders relaxed again on returning to guard.
messages.s_ed1156788a21c2165a33ee11fc4e6dc276fe78: I can rehearse the cover shape with comfortable vision without claiming to have blocked an impact.
messages.s_f6732b47f7c3c0edc3177d9cf690ecb8401756: Keep the hands lower within a comfortable range or practise the cover without stepping.
messages.s_140954ff6bfb3b3bab163ab1fbec8a287d7a03: Stop if neck or shoulder tension becomes painful or breathing is restricted.
messages.s_bc55cf2e2e144123507926819960c7a5266cdf: Original front and side close views show sightline, relaxed shoulders and return to guard.
messages.s_a3133e39b9d1322f75a5eaf96880e69678df80: Distinguish a rear-hand catch from a short outside parry against an imagined jab.
messages.s_74270f2b9ab7d7fae99accffc7672fc34923a7: Begin in your stance and imagine a slow jab toward the chin. For the catch, turn the rear palm toward that line close to its guard position; do not reach out.
messages.s_1c01cbb8cb1a23034a5b5aa0466e55d6f7ec10: Rehearse a small receiving shape with the rear forearm behind the hand. The front hand stays in guard; there is no punch or contact to catch here.
messages.s_49443d159c13e6874791a0eccf6ce913dafb07: For the outside parry, use the rear hand again: guide it a short distance across the imagined jab line toward the front shoulder, with a small controlled turn. Avoid a wide sweep or pulling the head back.
messages.s_e7bab34791e7535079062dae0da1221934690d: Bring the rear hand back to the cheek and reset after either shape. This planned solo drill does not teach reacting to a real punch; live timing needs supervised partner instruction.
messages.s_8789938af303fda0fd0a939a2147cf411b8bfd: Do not turn a catch or parry into a large arm swing. Name a small receive-release and a small redirect-return separately.
messages.s_aabb45fd40e11a8198603df0bb6c580c5b88bf:
Do five small rear-hand catches, then five rear-hand outside parries against an imagined jab. Pause at guard after each and name which shape receives and which redirects.

Short focused practice: Rehearse two slow catches and two redirects, each starting and ending at rear-hand guard, then explain their difference in your own words. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Swap catch and redirect order and stop in full guard after each.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit A relaxed guard; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_799e41013fcc4cd95a06b53150a8f5bfffb59b: I could distinguish receiving from redirecting without a wide hand sweep.
messages.s_4937e8543c1f005f68f652bd2af1291e015c0e: The front hand stayed in guard and the rear hand returned after each shape.
messages.s_5b93cb94fbc67b1bb0b5f8c462502653abe9cc: I can distinguish both shapes and return through a small path without testing them against a real punch.
messages.s_19ce7795033b9fa19bb7984c82f06b423a2673: Use even smaller hand motions or keep the elbow supported if upper-limb movement is limited.
messages.s_4e737378360b587122f8cd41e1d4600d5eca07: Stop if the shoulder or wrist hurts; do not add an untrained partner strike.
messages.s_3fee922920a40c8e8cd2c5d78f54d4b56a9a0e: Show two labeled rear-hand shapes from front and side: catch near guard, then short outside parry toward the front shoulder. Keep the front guard visible and show the reset. Use an imagined jab line only, without contact or successful-defence claims.
messages.s_c49733ea10eeada29462f748ecb88f7e60c947: Move the head slightly off an imagined straight line while staying over the feet.
messages.s_b2e2022df7ad2e81c87f8ba9b1660f5e328bf3: With eyes ahead and guard available, shift a little through ankles, knees and torso to one side; keep the bend modest.
messages.s_d9330d786338462bccdf321aab18bf74359325: Return to the middle, then try the other side. Avoid dropping the head below the hands or folding sharply at the waist.
messages.s_95b6e057f32ad7c84010a43525fd1ebfaff030: Do not confuse a slip with deep waist folding or a large sideways fall. Reduce the movement, keep the eyes open and return to the comfortable middle base.
messages.s_dc1173a85c182035ad329be28a765324cabf39:
Make three slow left-middle-right-middle sequences, with a breath and reset between them.

Short focused practice: Try two slow left-middle-right-middle cycles, stopping in the middle each time to check the feet and easy breathing. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a small right-middle-left-middle order instead of left-middle-right-middle.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Find your stance; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_22e91eb12cea116f8a3d07e6fc8ef016b609dc: I could stop at either side without falling forward.
messages.s_d19e2c7586493fad0fed976883c625624ec64b: My eyes and guard stayed oriented ahead.
messages.s_aea248bc86ef64ce459e17d61b22bbd392df22: I can distinguish the two small directions and return to the middle base without a large bend.
messages.s_e9f2ed37fd59981969048eda5ac44fc1429065: Use a very small weight shift or skip the head movement if neck or balance symptoms make it unsuitable.
messages.s_c6e75c20b7d076d37bb7af25f848a66c8e41f3: Stop for dizziness, headache, neck pain or loss of balance.
messages.s_65beee41bb880ee208b7820e22cd823ed6b495: Original front wide view marks centre and two modest positions; avoid a large dramatic head drop.
messages.s_acb24dfed2cf0c9c60677d02bf891f42a4b37b: Link a small bend and side shift without twisting or rushing.
messages.s_f92b693588940f524add502fe754dd3f73aba7: From guard, soften knees a little, move under an imagined high arc, then stand back into a stable stance on the other side.
messages.s_159241091b296d4dece93e16a241dcb2291d77: Keep the arc small and the back comfortable. This rehearses a movement path, not proof that a real hook was avoided.
messages.s_d7f4462cea7642b011d62808338611e155c1d4: Do not create the roll shape through a deep squat or neck twisting. Use a small imagined arc and move the torso together with comfortable knee motion.
messages.s_0d2784f5bc48069a0d99505c12661f6a164a9f:
Try four slow half-rolls each way with a full upright reset after every one.

Short focused practice: Choose two small half-arcs each way and rebuild guard and a comfortable base after each. If uncomfortable, rehearse the direction change with a small step only. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a small side step after the half-arc with a guard reset between them.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Small slips; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_1673b89de4bbe5d02e135ee2e38d76de0ca6ad: My feet stayed separated and my head returned over the base.
messages.s_21b8040603bd6f38d5cfd9b8bf0bfd2f448bad: I could breathe and stop anywhere in the path.
messages.s_6de1afb8ae638c999219b86ead1487f7f3cf6f: I can reduce the arc and explain that this is not a test of evading a real hook.
messages.s_61ee3edc24164b9eebc620fff70db788c795dd: Replace the roll with a small lateral step if bending is uncomfortable; there is no required depth.
messages.s_93498bc919c5e28642907b471aa432ee4576aa: Stop for dizziness or knee, back or neck pain; do not force a low duck.
messages.s_8dd026ae51d47641791f7e8ff0383bff8ec23d: Original wide side view of a modest arc and final stance, with no exact depth or avoidance score.
messages.s_b0d528bcca866391084272457be5a7415d890f: Introduce hooks and uppercuts as controlled solo shapes after straight punches and a reliable return to guard.
messages.s_95085561166ca765593c42c6b74455a7cbf406: Trace a compact lead-hand arc with the body turning together.
messages.s_6d30d4d5872f68f94c69afd22d3a7cf9a4ce58: From guard, rotate comfortably through the feet and trunk as the lead hand traces a short arc toward an imagined side target.
messages.s_fa4ed1bbd063037d8f3120a9ee7fd17805da50: Keep the wrist comfortable and the elbow neither pinned against the ribs nor thrown far behind. Return the hand and stance together.
messages.s_fc5c07466d9709ddd8e973d6d86dfda1285cb8: Do not start the lead hook by winding the arm back into a large swing. Choose a short comfortable arc from guard, keep the rear hand ready and return to the base.
messages.s_60cebcd0358b9f372d819c2693b10f39cbfea8:
Trace six slow lead hooks in the air with a full guard pause between repetitions.

Short focused practice: Try two short groups of three slow lead-hook shapes, stopping completely after each. Focus on the start in the first group and recovery in the second. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a familiar small exit after one lead hook without adding a long combination.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit A relaxed guard; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_f23b07da6aa593c59ed02eb230135c43bd52f3: The arc stayed compact rather than swinging the whole arm behind me.
messages.s_0cba3b535a53550a8b56d8d785c3ff137dbf1b: The rear hand and final stance remained available.
messages.s_46e55c085a5363dda2d3eda3d4aeda687ae024: I can distinguish the hook path from a straight and recover without a large wind-up.
messages.s_0e0965f17eb6d234f4f6317c8c159b614e1375: Make a smaller arc or rehearse only the gentle body turn if the arm path is uncomfortable.
messages.s_f2907d0894f97fd5b5d70900f9165f4141cc92: Stop for wrist, elbow, shoulder, back or knee pain; do not strike a bag with an unreviewed shape.
messages.s_9b75f68e26f80ffb3761bef6b25a81573a89ce: Original overhead hand arc and three-quarter body view; show return to guard, no elbow-angle number or impact.
messages.s_efe7e2747fac5c84b7a825d0a154915ec97ff0: Coordinate the rear-hand arc with a small turn and an intact lead guard.
messages.s_1977fa86f986032756cdadaca7e6351636b506: Begin in stance, let the rear foot and trunk turn comfortably, and draw a compact rear-hand arc across an imagined line.
messages.s_8e63956e615f2aaf996d754b9b1b6de1baef0c: Keep the lead hand near guard. Let the rear hand return before moving the feet again; do not over-rotate past a balanced base.
messages.s_c1d1f8fe4b91ea7409a0b8a6f8a1e7dfc685c0: Learn the rear hook without forcing it to be an exact reverse copy of the lead hook. Watch lead-hand readiness and comfortable base recovery during the small rear arc.
messages.s_a457f8b2a24fac7baf5e6ceb432d03e75f3084:
Practise four very slow rear hooks, reset, then four more from the opposite lead stance.

Short focused practice: Split the existing four slow repetitions into two pairs, lowering the hands to rest between them. If changing stance, name the new rear hand first. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: If choosing to change stance, name the new rear hand and use only one reduced rehearsal.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Find your stance; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_1358b45b3e4772b33bab95c8ae23bf69e0795d: The opposite hand did not leave guard.
messages.s_4e43a153196e905127116d3785c86e523d3ac1: I ended able to stop and step, without spinning.
messages.s_4b9b94bc91378d403b83acf2c03a784cb9b322: I know the difference between physical left-right and lead-rear hands and can recover comfortably from the rear hook.
messages.s_b10d817ca2169cf3252c264531ce173a2bcbb5: Reduce both the turn and arm arc if coordination or joint comfort is limited.
messages.s_100f1bf162c95adbc3e508e962c1c221f15554: Stop if rotational pain appears or you need an uncontrolled extra step.
messages.s_e7ee8d55669ce046ea2764acfe7a80faabb2c7: Original rear three-quarter shot with small foot-turn inset and static guard-hand marker.
messages.s_57286f86bc3907f3f50a1eac7edca14af3293b: Lift a compact lead-hand path without dropping the hand far below guard.
messages.s_3aa09682f1782d4f306f8a9b25dbc37ca585d4: Start with the lead hand near guard. Soften the knees a little, then let the hand rise on a short imagined inside line as the body returns upright.
messages.s_8fbd8b9dd70f7e480a52dcae5fbaafd288dc99: Do not swing from behind the hip or snap the elbow. Bring the hand back to guard before another repetition.
messages.s_9960ea10a193d02592cd9f3be82091036f0e5b: Do not start the lead uppercut by dropping the hand behind the hip for a large upward swing. Choose a short comfortable rise from lead guard and keep the rear hand ready.
messages.s_ca1d0bec80b06233f727f112d0e85dcc697c0f:
Perform six slow lead uppercut paths at a comfortable height with a full reset.

Short focused practice: Use three slow small lead-uppercut shapes for rise-return-stop, then optionally choose three more after a short rest. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a small back exit after the lead uppercut while retaining its short rise.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit A relaxed guard; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_baa930c4082aea0c18c6520a04cde279e0cdbc: The hand began and ended close to guard.
messages.s_d6c646c88d2f3656f8ca62d9e49f3a3ed22839: The knees softened without a deep or painful dip.
messages.s_5f075e9a92f72951231509141c868b76760b5c: I can distinguish the short rising path from a hook arc and return without a large wind-up.
messages.s_33c6f8e25a5b5c187f6445aea946224a53875f: Use a smaller rise or omit the knee bend if it is uncomfortable.
messages.s_a5fc98e99314cbde46c33e8301c0f7b437523f: Stop for knee, back, shoulder, elbow or wrist pain; do not force a low starting position.
messages.s_abbb93cd107700023093e1071081ffa731a5b3: Original side and front views show short upward hand path from guard, without a deep dip or impact target.
messages.s_908085f54742423023220955d2af3378c3334d: Use a compact rear-hand rising path while keeping the lead guard.
messages.s_04b4473b45d04e43c2ac6ea0cfd5ee23f82737: Begin with both hands ready. Allow a small rear-side turn and a gentle knee-softening while the rear hand rises close to the torso.
messages.s_4264d81a792c8494079785593956e5711809b9: Finish without throwing the shoulder upward or reaching far past the stance; return the rear hand and settle the feet.
messages.s_83f55091fc613bae224850905a96d1742835aa: Do not jump the head upwards or squeeze the shoulder toward the ear in a rear uppercut. Reduce the rise, keep the foot-and-torso turn comfortable and leave the lead hand ready.
messages.s_0ea0fbb8c55f5195ce993312e59d6e5cd8dff9:
Make five rear uppercut paths slowly and pause after each to check the lead hand.

Short focused practice: Watch only the short rise in the first two slow repetitions and only recovery in the next two; choose a fifth if comfortable. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Rehearse the rear uppercut separately after a small direction change.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Recover after the rear straight; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_77203ee27986bbbeacba5d569e40e02d2295d8: The lead hand stayed available near guard.
messages.s_bad20f468adb04f104bdb3aa9442415299cf57: The movement finished balanced, not leaning behind the target.
messages.s_ab702432ee0ef9a4f145cdcb63bf79973f9733: I can rehearse the rear uppercut through a small path and finish with a comfortable base and ready lead hand.
messages.s_f79f05b15ff1320538b150ed9e66a015f0dd0a: Keep the rear turn minimal or rehearse the hand path alone if the coordinated move is uncomfortable.
messages.s_f0a8755e8c64a649193422654bd527ed4c860a: Stop for back, knee or upper-limb pain, or if you must hold your breath to finish.
messages.s_5ad59491c2ee3f783b42caa4b0d0fd25024b6c: Original rear-side and front split view: short inside rising path, lead guard and final reset.
messages.s_d1cc95a37efd6e11bf0602cc52133231fce3b2: Distinguish head and body lines without changing into a reach or a deep bend.
messages.s_51f5cf78758143dccceaf9b318cb204f00e876: Visualise two empty points at different heights. For the lower point, soften knees slightly and redirect the path while keeping the head over the feet.
messages.s_016ead4f700e712f4844d3d1c61ce425c5c9d9: Alternate one comfortable straight at the higher line and one controlled curved shape at the lower line. Never punch a person or object.
messages.s_24db993bfe9db61944df02de332d2efcbdd6f3: Do not reach a low imagined target by forcing the arm and folding at the waist. Move the target closer, reduce the level change and keep the head over the base.
messages.s_c3a31957c1afb3db60a7dd08fbe8e2965e798e:
Trace four high-low pairs with a guard reset after each pair and no demand for exact height.

Short focused practice: Use the same slow punch path for two high-low pairs and stop in full guard after each level. Choose the remaining pairs only while comfortable. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Swap the target-level order without adding a real object.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Enter and leave range; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_92791b38b776941bca1cd8abeee0040c15b714: I changed level without falling over the lead foot.
messages.s_f47798ad0357225e6f0082413e3f7463c69fd6: The hands returned to guard after both paths.
messages.s_6bfaa39091bcc0122344a389f6bb571e50c7b5: I can change an imagined target level comfortably and know this is not a real accuracy test.
messages.s_e35e6e533513a90b0ee9b7fe4354982aed29f5: Choose two closer, comfortable imaginary levels or keep both at the same level if bending is unsuitable.
messages.s_6991f16e208d810ae22f37a5f306de2ae0e019: Stop if lowering the target produces knee, back or shoulder pain.
messages.s_80413ce815c239e0f2f820572268e20778e48d: Original side view marks two imagined empty target lines and a modest body-level change; no numerical angle or hit animation.
messages.s_8a7de3228d05e08f021cb9b6240de510ab1329: Join familiar shapes in short, explainable sequences; each ends with guard and balance.
messages.s_b2046273b5ce5e433f79184a58c054684e23c0: Use the second jab as a separate action before the rear straight.
messages.s_3a9ed70bdfbfbd6a94961f849bc5f935630b9d: Send jab, return, jab, return, then rear straight. Count the three starts from guard aloud while learning.
messages.s_8d46e13584eeba5f139edb2991ced3520dd21d: Keep the feet quiet and the rear hand ready during both jabs. After the rear straight, bring it home before stepping away.
messages.s_aa01f51cf148baf8b28baa81a11e208af5ce1c: Skipping the second jab or shortening returns confuses the three-punch sequence. Separate jab-return-jab-return-rear straight-return first, then connect comfortably.
messages.s_3522addc3fe758c4782225184b00c0072dd4fa:
Perform five slow three-punch sequences, each followed by a backward exit and full reset.

Short focused practice: Say and pause through the first two triples, then connect the next two comfortably and finish with a small back exit. The last attempt is optional. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a small side exit rather than back after the triple, recovering the hands first.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Two jabs, one base; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_1ca5e5f0b1e17aee8d62003cfbb821f458179d: I could pause between the two jabs without losing the sequence.
messages.s_075310e48f75b9e782ce99c107b74c2fe64c18: Only one hand left guard at a time.
messages.s_956b92a1ab0e03652aa285ff0d6e641d3502e1: I know how a double-jab sequence differs from a one-two and can return to the base after the triple.
messages.s_dbd030ba3d6aa51cced0e29bfb13333824487c: Add a full guard pause between every action or return to the two-jab lesson.
messages.s_79834d3233e19c2b8bd7a165262889cc6403b6: Stop when pace makes the hands hang low or the exit becomes unsafe.
messages.s_2685a8d581f5e2b9d07adbde9599fb6c117432: Original wide three-quarter sequence with 1-1-2 captions and a clearly visible backward exit, no order score.
messages.s_780e5c36419f554ccc378495f9787c795c3c4a: Add one compact curved action after two controlled straights.
messages.s_7370d5d8e62eec9f8db196c51f62994a6fc6dd: Jab and return, rear straight and return, then draw the lead hook arc. Keep each action distinct before linking the rhythm.
messages.s_38c9bc8fe9b162ef6aa04bd7f663377d8d79c2: The hook begins from a recovered lead guard, not from a hand left extended after the jab. End with both hands ready.
messages.s_94e9a49f3f95794db731385b8e0fe93cf1d000: Do not swing a wide hook before recovering from the rear straight. Separate the three paths with pauses first and keep a short lead hook with rear-hand readiness when connecting them.
messages.s_9bfb37b39ad469b009971dc5479e1160cb35c8:
Trace four slow 1-2-hook sequences with a complete rest and stance reset between them.

Short focused practice: Use two paused one-two-lead-hook sequences, then choose two connected attempts after a short break. Rebuild the final guard each time. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Change the exit direction after the same triple without enlarging the hook path.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Jab then rear straight; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_48fc2cef7964bdf0d9d09038c50849a19c010f: The hook was compact rather than an arm swing from behind.
messages.s_824b926ec744cdc310bd2834ea76855efe56d2: My stance could support a step after the third action.
messages.s_28659a1ca0448866a2bccf8d3811a353806788: I can distinguish the straight and arc paths in order and return both hands to readiness after the triple.
messages.s_a6dceb5a6a9613ea4000fd2c392445a8cbb0e6: Practise 1-2 alone or use a smaller final arc until the sequence is comfortable.
messages.s_9cec0bf6a1de8fe3475c0604b21fbe84dd33e8: Stop for shoulder, elbow or rotational pain, or when the third action pulls you off balance.
messages.s_07853f7331dc2e457e688140dee2f7091571cc: Original three-quarter demonstration with separate jab, rear straight, compact hook frames and full guard recovery.
messages.s_93eaaf26fd53f9a07732c38fa2d0e3d638d51b: Follow two straights with a small inside rising path while retaining balance.
messages.s_594d1a35e113553a5b52f4157d4c9f7d82ec7e: Complete the jab and rear straight as separate actions. After the rear hand returns, soften the knees slightly and lift the lead hand on its short inside line.
messages.s_a3d2e14d531a9f89287da08a50bcd4da3db747: Do not dive forward to create the uppercut. Return upright with the lead hand back at guard.
messages.s_559439a306fc214a93f58d762f7e7c2e68e095: Do not dive forwards or pull the hand back to add the uppercut. Recall the short lead rise separately first, then add it comfortably after the one-two.
messages.s_1d6f8e6c7134f6fe3116df9fd5c8a8632046c8:
Make four careful sequences at a speaking pace; pause after each to check both knees and hands.

Short focused practice: Recall one lead-uppercut recovery, then use two paused and optionally two connected one-two-lead-uppercut sequences, stopping in the full base each time. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose a different familiar small exit after the triple and keep the rising path short.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Jab then rear straight; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_41999e8506fdea0e025600009d5986399740a3: The uppercut started near guard, not below the waist.
messages.s_60906a063c204c6a2f43cf8234832107397c8a: I could stop after the third action without an extra step.
messages.s_72bae19f1556d36cc3066f88bf054b92cbf4be: I can explain the difference between adding a hook arc and adding a rising path to the sequence.
messages.s_2433ddc676953e157ca1beb53494188119738a: Replace the uppercut with a short lead-hand reach or omit the knee movement if uncomfortable.
messages.s_bd36477b7014a4c487d3e864c6d8b8d152301d: Stop for back, knee or arm pain, or if breathing becomes strained.
messages.s_ba32e58fb37592bfb5607132fa3876671db372: Original side and front split view distinguishes the straight line from the final short rising line; no impact.
messages.s_df7ae65f9895b5054a1db5b45a7bf638528c86: Rehearse a small exit followed by a single straight without claiming reaction skill.
messages.s_3c7eeccd0feb33eb7578cc1e6d5fbda90227ee: Choose the sequence before starting: cover, diagonal step, reset, jab. Move on your own cue; nobody is attacking.
messages.s_98d9970c27e5b9bef7e7bf12ec530003fde6bd: The step must end in balance before the jab. Finish with a hand return and a backward exit.
messages.s_39f2c69243c67937a99592616017114c5f465c: Do not rush a punch immediately after the planned cover. Rebuild the base with a small diagonal step first, then choose a slow jab and back exit.
messages.s_81ceb9a1519c97a9fc0a3265efc730474a4c94:
Do three rehearsals to each diagonal side, slowly enough to name all five parts.

Short focused practice: Speak the cover-diagonal step-reset-jab-back exit chain first, then use two slow rehearsals and revisit the hardest connection once separately. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Change only the diagonal direction in the chain without testing defence against a real attack.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Compact cover; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_10c91fb7b3b47e07cc812a1dea53288700264a: I did not punch while still falling into the step.
messages.s_90f3067ebe180ccbcf198aeed27cf4414e8d85: I understand this does not test response to a real opponent.
messages.s_b5f30bee6c9e50b64daa47462cd4ed05b1e779: I can establish the base between the defensive shape and return action and understand this as planned rehearsal.
messages.s_7c0c193ff3be50b3aa95e306335ad4b438e64c: Use cover-step-reset only, without a punch, if the full chain is tiring or uncomfortable.
messages.s_c22c21c12b4e123342d3779a1cff04665e2b4e: Stop if you rush into an obstacle or the sequence causes pain or dizziness.
messages.s_ac294b901f38358160624687a4c81699090a0e: Original wide floor diagram shows a self-cued five-step sequence; no opponent, incoming strike or reflex score.
messages.s_2fc469a17b62367b864ca842f03a7adedd04ff: Finish a short combination by changing the line and restoring guard.
messages.s_f14a391fe51b6f4e7e28f481c076742d365f0a: Choose either jab-cross or jab-jab-cross. After the last hand returns, make one small side step or pivot to an open line.
messages.s_3929caba3573a9976302a2a34cce170c0a7c3a: Keep the exit separate at first. Count 'hands home, then feet' to avoid moving with both hands away.
messages.s_01aa919b7c482d30dd8372b0f75c6b12a660f2: Do not try to leave through a large pivot before finishing the combination. Return the hands first, then choose a small side step or comfortable turn.
messages.s_dd0683ae5563f91bf60d2f84f11efb99fec7a8:
Perform five combinations, alternating a side-step and a modest pivot exit.

Short focused practice: Try a side exit after the one-two twice, then a small-turn option after the same sequence twice, and choose the comfortable path yourself. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Keep the straight sequence the same and alternate the side-step and small-turn exits.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Side steps; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_d47e5e8273bab3eaed872fbe55a0f780a6151e: Both hands were back before my exit began.
messages.s_c854f5f1bb95cfad88dd085c4d51ea98064d32: The exit ended in a stance I could continue from.
messages.s_451fe1213ca61b9856f740c62a4167e53b4dc0: I can sequence the combination, hand recovery and exit and choose the exit path deliberately.
messages.s_68c156a058d67b54b7ae5739481548f319d0e1: Choose the side step instead of pivoting if rotation is uncomfortable; reduce the combination to one jab.
messages.s_07ff37593eab863d02d3895afe89c8828c6c69: Stop if the exit crosses the feet, approaches an obstacle, or causes joint pain.
messages.s_bad03760f3086afac4533047fef5e418b0edb5: Original overhead path and wide performer view show clear punch-return-exit phases with no success score.
messages.s_dc3324589682516aaa5ee7b86a686b96d6d09c: Apply a small number of cues in short solo rounds. Time is a practice aid, not a fitness or technique score.
messages.s_e7a936b38dee143c0ad40e14203e59e8836040: Keep one simple theme for a short interval without chasing a punch count.
messages.s_229be40ba3542e99a162e29e0170ec0b7992c5: At every new solo session, recheck the clear, stable space. Start with easy general movement, then rehearse familiar stance, small steps and light jab-and-guard returns; build gradually only while breathing and control stay comfortable.
messages.s_13f66c590fd8990e5fc610f8074d52c5be8bb9: Choose jab and guard return as the only theme. Work for up to one easy minute, pausing whenever the shape or breathing changes.
messages.s_e78a86a15cc59014bd7e3e3ef5eb03d56f1a93: Rest and reflect on one cue only. A round is useful even when you stop early; quality does not require a fixed number of punches.
messages.s_5352d9c6ee2ca6ebf04e757aa726c48b003b40: Do not abandon jab recovery or guard just to fill the time. Pausing or ending earlier is valid; this round has only one jab-return focus.
messages.s_7356597f38105b4d740616c9ea123ae9667428: When the planned work ends comfortably, lower the pace with familiar slow steps and easy breathing before resting and noting one observation. If a stop signal appears, stop immediately instead of tapering.
messages.s_931250f9a0da6277de4c9c9b94150f186262e8:
Try one 60-second ceiling round with optional pauses, then name one action you could repeat.

Short focused practice: Choose a short section of at most 20 seconds first, rest and optionally try another with the same focus. The existing 60 seconds is a ceiling, not a completion target. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose jab recovery rather than the straight path as the next short section's single focus.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit The jab comes home; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_0f57869ac8564275f31579163cc771cfeacfc8: I kept the chosen theme clear instead of adding extra techniques.
messages.s_dc9f7e548e3ce7c24606e272f391ebf40577f0: I took a pause when breathing or control asked for it.
messages.s_ce62033e66b0cf631d7baba0e134e500761398: I can remember the chosen jab-return focus through the round and stop when it becomes confused.
messages.s_1dfff382b600e5f03bef04dc49185b46fd4986: Work for 20-30 seconds or replace punches with guard and easy steps if needed.
messages.s_f1296ceb9418f67f37380f1efa7ce650ab927e: Stop for dizziness, chest pain, unusual breathlessness or a sudden technique breakdown.
messages.s_4dc7a5dc8c5e5f6b8759fa2803a1d863a73069: Original single fixed wide shot and simple optional timer; no punch score, fatigue estimate or dramatic impact.
messages.s_9a1afc40a156535fe93c3c1cebb26bf5df64cc: Sustain a short planned footwork pattern without crossing the feet.
messages.s_f705653b012192e47db233f9138f582e4fa150: At every new solo session, recheck the clear, stable space. Start with easy general movement, then rehearse familiar stance, small steps and guard returns without punches; build gradually only while breathing and control stay comfortable.
messages.s_0eb84a937646ba4f0c49a47f281eb4d570c0b1: Choose forward, back, side, reset as a four-part loop. Keep hands in guard and use no punches for this round.
messages.s_8b1693272f3721fc44cb77e8ce817b96c3a342: Move slowly enough to stop after any step. Change direction only after the base is restored.
messages.s_fd1d3136e247e75627ee4f6c363af06e98695e: Adding punches or constantly circling one way changes the movement-round focus. Plan small forward-back and side paths and check the base in each section.
messages.s_e397c1c8ce1c14831e5ca7f1545d3027e33e8f:
Repeat the loop for up to one minute, then pause and note where spacing drifted.

Short focused practice: Choose a forward-back pair and a side pair and use only those paths for a section of at most 20 seconds. Rest and recall the path order; continuing is optional. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Swap the same foot paths' order in the next short section.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Forward and back; check only the confusing part again.
messages.s_eb386c44e952faf401634d6f07e69e7ed2ce1b: I could stop balanced after every segment.
messages.s_6a70fd8dde7f705ea28217b30b32de32dbc02d: I noticed and corrected foot spacing before moving again.
messages.s_b4ad323289c44329148a439609a344c1240e5c: I can change foot paths without adding punches and attend to stance spacing at each transition.
messages.s_c1c3955c07a2026d01f0ae0436bcefb865dd6c: Use a smaller loop or weight shifts only when travel space or balance is limited.
messages.s_239026af2fc2a0917eb3b763ff66ca80f20c59: Stop if you stumble, the floor becomes slippery, or joint pain appears.
messages.s_0852b304b26c235bbb861bd0ba6d14be1b230b: Original overhead four-direction floor loop and wide front stance view; no footwork grade.
messages.s_e29fa44e99c1f6914a84bf4ecd440601388d6f: Choose a consistent empty target line without increasing reach to chase it.
messages.s_20483b3c0330883ab8860634fe5820542094b9: Pick a point in empty air within comfortable reach. Use a jab, rear straight and pause in guard while keeping eyes on the same point.
messages.s_f0e2c8e91a59927db8ed5bc9e1fcfaa1a16123: If you would need to lean, take a small step first and reset. Accuracy here is your own path check, not a camera-measured hit.
messages.s_db4c2a7fca350f33eaacbaaee106e6ab68d24c: Do not lean far or strike an object while following an imagined target. Choose a point within comfortable reach and reset the base when it changes.
messages.s_5c750202ec5bd4711511b87005e1479ffd3f64:
Work up to 45 seconds on one target, then change to another comfortable empty point for a second short set.

Short focused practice: Choose three slow straight paths toward one imagined point, stop and name a second comfortable point. Three more toward the new point are optional. Rest between sections; take longer if you need it.

When comfortable, try changing just one variable: Choose the second comfortable point along a different reach direction and rebuild the base.

Next practice: At the next suitable session, recall the short sequence without reading first. Briefly revisit Enter and leave range; check only the confusing part again.

messages.s_4cc7f4896f82c7829af98ce1892e34195b8dc1: Write support (H2 or optional H1), sequence (A or C), arm alternative (S B/omit), half/full cycle and stop reasons. Example: H2 A once; rest; S B left hand only; finish for pain/dizziness/unsafe balance. Choose for your needs rather than copying the example. B reference: in S, 1–2 bring one hand a small comfortable distance forward (no higher than lower chest), 3–4 return to thigh; repeat separately with other hand. Do not release H2 hands. A: 1–2 very small loading change left, 3–4 centre, 5–6 very small loading change right, 7–8 centre/rest. H2; soles down. Do not imitate by side bending/reaching a shoulder; small whole-body displacement may occur. No loading percentage/full single-leg target. With both hands supported and both soles in contact, begin by moving your body as a whole a very small distance left; allow slightly more loading on the left without fully unloading the right leg. Return to the comfortable starting centre through the same small whole-body movement. Reverse the directions for the right side. Do not imitate by sideways waist bending; there is no loading-percentage or exact-alignment target.

messages.s_18d10eaf030b5e680720d18d7516df32b272a2: These lessons teach the observed order and visible hand/foot paths. Quarter, half and three-quarter turns label the geometry of the visible heading changes; they are not measured joint angles or compass bearings. A foot staying near the same floor location does not establish a heel pivot or a load percentage. There is no instruction to lock a foot to the floor. Sole contact, loading, knee forces and a suitable pain-free personal range were not measured. Cropping at 9, foot occlusion at 12 and arm/foot overlap at 16 are flagged separately. Do not fill hidden fist height or wrist rotation by guessing. Stop a physical attempt if you cannot move comfortably; you can continue written recall. Stopping interrupts that attempt and does not complete a physical kata. The reference was viewed muted: this course does not claim to teach heard kiai, breathing rhythm or spoken commands.
messages.s_c9e7b5b9c6b1748357ee88dab06b8b9b50b0ff: N is your initial ready heading; E is your initial right, W your initial left, and S behind. These are not screen sides. In recording A, the bow at 0:02.4 has close heels, outward-pointing toes and open hands beside the thighs; the instructor is upright at 0:04.3. To open into ready, the left foot moves outward first at 0:05.3, then the right moves outward while the forearms cross in front at 0:06.4. At 0:07.5–0:12.0 the feet are apart, toes outward and closed fists low in front of the thighs. Learn this order: bow–upright–left outward–right outward with crossed arms–ready. Continue directly into count 1; add no boxing guard. Foot width, pressure and a suitable personal stance depth were not measured from this observation. B starts already ready; do not attribute an opening bow to it.
messages.s_85ca135d9c70e3245da35a9e1f41dfd723b63d: Begin from A’s left-punch/left-front finish at 0:41.6. At 0:43.2 the left foot moves inward and the left arm folds high while the torso returns toward the initial heading. At 0:43.8 the forearms are crossed and the original heading restored; ready follows at 0:45.3. Frame stepping at 0:46.3–0:46.8 shows the left foot closing inward first, then the right joining it as the hands open beside the thighs. The bow is at 0:48.8 and upright at 0:50.1. Learn this closing order: recover with the left foot and restore the initial heading–cross arms–ready–left inward–right joins–open hands–bow–upright. This A-specific foot order is not assigned to B’s unseen interval. Travel distance, sole contact and exact return to an original floor point were not measured. Add no 21st punch or intervening boxing guard.

messages.s_4d9a978a5240c741e32275c8302a5865d54a07:
Stand where you can take two steps in any direction without hitting anything. Prop the phone at about waist height, leaning on something solid — a chair, a shelf, a wall.

Then step back until your feet and your hands both fit in the picture at the same time. That is the whole test. If your feet leave the frame when you punch, you are too close.

Turn slightly toward the camera rather than standing square to it. A boxing guard is side-on, and from directly in front your rear hand hides behind your body — the camera reads a hand it cannot see as a hand that is not there.

The room only needs enough light that you can see your own hands clearly. We do not measure the light, so we cannot tell you when it is too dark; you can.
messages.s_9d0c72c934d2f0eca7133112ef4299229d2c95:
Feet about shoulder width, lead foot forward, rear heel slightly lifted. Weight sits between your feet — not forward on the toes, not back on the heels.

Hands up: lead hand out around chin height, rear hand touching your cheek. The rear hand is the one that keeps you safe and the one that gets tired first. When it drops, you will hear about it.

Stay tall. The most common fault in the first week is folding forward at the waist to reach further — it feels stronger and it takes your balance with it.

We can see stance width, crossed feet and balance, and we grade those. We can see your guard hand and we will tell you when it drops, but we do not put a number on it: experienced coaches disagree about where exactly it belongs.
messages.s_7a8f8b5564978f03aeedac446cf903201cea67:
The jab is your lead hand, travelling straight out and straight back on the same line. It is not a big punch. It is the one that measures distance and buys you time.

Push from the floor, turn the shoulder, let the arm follow. Fist finishes where your eyes are pointing. Elbow stays down and behind the fist — when the elbow swings out to the side, the punch stops being a jab.

The return matters as much as the punch. A hand that comes back slowly is a hand that is not home when it is needed. We do not call this one out today — watch for it yourself.

Throw them at a pace you can hold. Speed that costs you shape is not speed — it is a faster way to practise something you do not want.
messages.s_ecf849910c0eed075a58d3ae35411a2efb20ae:
Both hands stay in front of your face and the punches leave from there. Lead hand out around chin height, rear hand touching your cheek. Elbows down and in — a guard held with the elbows out looks tighter than it is, because the hands are up and the middle is open.

This lesson is jabs, but the jab is not the point. The point is what the other hand does while the jab is away, and what the jab hand does on the way back.

The rear hand is the first thing fatigue takes. It drifts down a few centimetres at a time and it does not feel like anything happening. Throw slowly enough that you can feel it stay.

We can see both hands during the punch, and we call it out when the rear hand drops. A slow return on the lead hand is a real fault too, but we do not call that one out today. Neither carries a number: experienced coaches disagree about exactly where the guard belongs, so what fires is a flag, not a score.
messages.s_de7e528c110566a1c5391ca953280d493e5d2b:
Two things go wrong when a punch has to travel further than it should. The elbow swings out to find a shortcut, and the body leans in to cover the distance.

The elbow first. A straight punch keeps the elbow under and behind the fist for as long as it can. When the elbow lifts out to the side, the fist arrives on a curve — wider, slower, and no longer the punch you were practising.

Then the lean. If you have to fall forward to land, you were not in range. Reaching puts your weight over your lead foot and takes away the thing that lets you throw the next one.

The fix is under you, not in front of you. Step in, then punch. Range is a footwork problem wearing an arm problem's clothes.

We can see the elbow angle and the forward lean, and we call both out. Neither carries a number: the thresholds behind them are not calibrated, so you get the flag and not a score.
messages.s_7ad8abe21e6163d9ca533ed09e949897750e98:
The cross is the rear hand, and it travels a longer road: it starts further away and it has to cross your body to arrive. That distance is where its weight comes from and also where the trouble comes from.

Turn the rear foot and hip first, then the shoulder, then let the hand go. If the arm leads, you are throwing with your arm alone and reaching for the target with your chest.

Your lead hand does not go on holiday while the cross is out. It stays up. The most common shape fault here is one hand out and the other drifting down at the same time.

We cannot tell you how hard it lands. A camera sees shape and timing, not force, and we will not print a number we did not take.
messages.s_a6a8ca1f98755dad56a47f5b755a462b845f5d:
One is the jab, two is the cross. Thrown together, the jab is not just a punch — it is what makes room for the one behind it.

Let the jab come back before the cross goes out. The two punches share one line and one balance; if the second starts while the first is still travelling, you end up leaning into the shot with both hands away from your face.

Land back in your stance, not past it. Finishing a combination out of position is how a good pair of punches becomes a bad third one.

We watch the jab and the cross on their own, the same way we watch them everywhere else. Judging the two together as a combination — a wrong hand, a wrong order — is not something the app does today.
messages.s_13c85e77865bb65d8d5f39fd01ed46411c750c:
Three minutes, one round, nothing to reach. The only goal is to keep the shape you have been practising while the clock runs and your arms start to complain.

Work at a pace you could hold for a second round even though there is not one. If you are throwing so fast that your hands stop coming home, you are practising the fault, not the punch.

Somewhere around the two minute mark the rear hand starts to sit lower. That is not a character flaw, it is fatigue, and it is exactly what a round is for: it shows you where your shape ends.

The clock runs whether or not the camera can read you. If it loses you, it will say so rather than go quiet.
messages.s_cf56dc6079bbf3f734e217f1447b6b53737ace:
Your stance does not survive movement by accident — it survives because you move it as one piece, not two.

Step with the foot closest to where you are going, and let the other foot follow the same distance. Moving forward: lead foot goes first, rear foot catches up to the width you started with. Moving back: rear foot goes first, lead foot catches up. Neither foot ever passes the other — the moment they cross, you have no base to punch from and none to defend from either.

Small steps beat big ones. A big step closes distance fast but leaves you standing on one foot a beat too long; a small step keeps both feet live the whole time you are moving.

Stay on the balls of your feet, not flat. Flat feet react a fraction of a second slower in every direction — forward, back, or out of the way.

We can see when your feet cross, and we call it out. What we do not see is whether the step itself was the right size or the right moment to take it — that is a coach's eye, not a camera's.
messages.s_a4eb0706d1505d218762cd3e64bea3a2b05f18:
The range lesson said it plainly: reaching is a footwork problem wearing an arm's clothes. This lesson is the footwork side of that sentence.

Close the distance first. Step until you are actually in range, let your foot land, and only then throw. A punch thrown while you are still moving forward borrows its power from momentum instead of your stance — it can land harder by accident and leaves you off balance by design.

The tell is what happens right after the punch lands. If your weight keeps travelling forward after the fist arrives, the step and the punch happened at the same time instead of one after the other. If you settle back into your stance instead, they were sequenced correctly.

This is not about slowing down. Fast fighters step and plant just as we describe here — the sequence is still step, then punch, only compressed into less time.

We can see when you lose your balance coming out of a punch, and we call it out. We cannot tell you whether that happened because you rushed the step or skipped it — only that your base was not there when the punch landed.
messages.s_e584bd8329b065d9d0f2685e14c6f1fb95fa2a:
Ten minutes, one round, no break — and the missing break is the point.

Rest resets the drift that fatigue puts into your timing, and that drift is exactly the thing this lesson is about. Break it into pieces and you measure a fresh boxer three times instead of a tiring one once.

Hold one pace. Not your fastest and not a crawl: the speed you could still be throwing at minute nine. Most people find it about two thirds of what they started with.

We read tempo from how long the punch takes to extend, not from how fast anything moves across the screen. That is why a slow arm close to the camera and a quick one far away do not fool it.

We do not judge whether the pace is costing your form — that call is yours to make.
messages.s_81c58d957aa833b091b990a4819ba490be8661:
One round, five minutes. Longer than a boxing round on purpose — this is conditioning, not a fight.

Somewhere past minute three the shape starts to go before the effort does. Hands sit a little lower, the return gets a little lazy, the feet stop resetting. Nothing dramatic, and that is why it is worth watching for.

When you notice it, do not speed up to make up for it. Slow down until the shape comes back. A clean minute is worth more here than two ragged ones.

No rest, because there is no second round to rest for.
messages.s_a55dbcdaaf79bca26854b7895f8d62bb56c629:
Ten minutes of work, split into three rounds with rest between them.

Two hundred seconds a round is arithmetic, not tradition: ten minutes of work, split three ways. It is worth knowing that the same sum, done independently for the twenty minute lesson, lands on the same round length.

The rest is a ratio borrowed from the three by three lesson, not something we measured. We are telling you that because a number you cannot check should at least come with a note saying where it came from.

Aim to finish round three looking like round one. That is the whole exercise.
messages.s_87b2929cf76f9824618d2987fa324982842d51:
Six rounds, twenty minutes of work. The longest thing in this course.

Sixty seconds between rounds — the corner-break convention, chosen rather than measured. Short enough that fatigue carries across, which is the point of a long session.

By round four you will find out which part of your shape goes first. For most people it is the rear hand, then the return, then the feet. Learning your own order is more useful than any score we could print.

Long enough that the app's own tracking gets tested too — it will tell you if it loses you.
messages.s_ec7ec7669a90530e38d9dd110f55c6ffb506a4:
Three rounds of three minutes, and the only kind of round where the form feedback stays on the whole time.

That makes it the slowest lesson here, and it should be. You are not trying to fit punches into the time; you are trying to make each one the same as the last.

There is a real tension in leaving feedback on continuously, and we would rather name it than hide it: being corrected on every repetition can make you lean on the correction instead of learning the movement. Today that tension is theoretical — the correction only appears when the camera can read you, and the shape of it will be worth revisiting once it does so on a real device.

Ninety seconds of rest, which is generous for the work. Here the rest is less about breath and more about resetting, so the next round starts from your shape rather than the last round's drift.
messages.s_103f7f16c9c6516b867daf92c8e827f03d80fc:
Four rounds of five minutes. Long rounds, deliberately — the same twenty minutes split into six shorter rounds would just be the twenty minute lesson again.

Do not change pace to survive it. The point is to hold one pace long enough that your technique, not your will, becomes the limit.

Sixty seconds of rest, kept short on purpose. Fatigue has to carry from one round to the next or there is no trend to see.

What you are looking for is not whether you finish. It is which thing goes first, and how early. That answer is yours and it does not need a number attached to it.
messages.s_f80356ab554de0b5a1e32a6fe7095f6805181b: Kicks are not in the rule set. The engine reads a striking stance and arm angles; a leg travelling at head height is a different measurement we have not built or checked against coaches.
messages.s_927efc49af99e066e0006f0bcbc984fdd34b32: Kata is a pattern across the floor over minutes. We track a body, not where that body is in a room over time, so the part that defines the form is the part we cannot see.
messages.s_a9e787733381459e6ea064063a097020803369: Elbows and knees live at a range where the limbs cross in front of the torso. That is the same overlap our confidence gate already refuses to judge in boxing — opening it would mean grading exactly the frames we throw away.
messages.s_4a798284a353c170f2070deddbe2079110aade: Spinning and jumping kicks leave the ground and turn. The engine reads one orientation per frame and is told to expect an upright body, so a spin is not a case it can read — and we have not built the second pass that would.
messages.s_1ff572fedb2a95002a2b233be83b9c89559904: This is a mix of three rule sets and we have one. Nothing here is hard in a new way — it is the boxing, kickboxing and Muay Thai work, added up, and none of the other two exist.
messages.s_caa20a0908884468987c8ae884924ff831902d: Solo forms are a good fit and the reference gap is the only thing between us. The dummy form stays out for a different reason: the dummy is equipment, and we track the body, not the object it is working against.
messages.s_80435e5df085feaba12ad8068ebc91681ecf1b: Grappling is defined by contact and resistance from another person. A solo camera sees neither, so any score would be invented.
messages.s_bb37d1ea80aea8ae4e8684de03ab68b379990f: Same reason as BJJ: the technique lives in the connection between two bodies. Solo drilling exists, but grading it would mean grading the half you can see.
messages.s_a2818f613015966b4b6e5995a8b4b5764115f5: Throws depend on your partner's balance and reaction. Uchikomi without a partner is a movement rehearsal, not the technique.
messages.s_c234ea7f2d15e9680e1c3c65e6de4ab1d4e5f4: The technique is defined by where the weapon is. Pose estimation tracks the body, not the object, so the part that matters most is invisible.
messages.s_1d4e62d060d7bc8f305e4613c92a23410dc8e1: Both need a second person. We support solo drills that prepare you for them, and we say clearly that this is not the same thing.
messages.s_309e517f70831c8bb3e56a95e8293612761d7a: We can help you train movement. Nobody can promise how a real situation goes, and an app that implies otherwise is doing you harm.
messages.s_560ac9d96972c64d58bf0d2894570aa9f15f09: We can see your head move. We cannot tell you whether it was the right move, because right is defined by a punch that isn't there. Grading a slip with nothing to slip would be grading a guess.
messages.s_a7ec488b6084c7fb2d6132adeb83410863cf25: We track your body, not the bag — so the thing a coach actually watches, how the bag moves, is invisible to us. Contact also changes what we do read: a punch that lands stops early and returns differently from one that travels free.
messages.s_45b04aa104e5e373aad98e330254b0cf8abedb: A phone across the room cannot hear you, and chest movement during boxing is mostly the boxing. Telling you to breathe on a schedule we cannot check would be advice dressed as feedback.
messages.s_2190d86378dca1ce49eb05b60b0bfb9a00533f: We read shape, not tissue. Nothing here can tell a sore shoulder from a tired one, and nothing here is medical advice. If something hurts, that decision belongs to you and a professional, not to a camera.
messages.s_851223a66dc54bfc72f08ba844221b3b683adc: That call weighs things we never see: how you take a shot, how you behave when tired and hit, who you would be in with. A number from solo practice cannot carry it, so we do not print one.

messages.s_62418a38c3e13215c469342505a196846f5a50:
Three rounds of three minutes, with ninety seconds of scheduled rest between rounds. That adds up to twelve planned minutes: nine working and three resting.

Choose a pace you can control from the first round. You do not have to maintain a pace that stops being comfortable or controlled.

Use the rest. Ninety seconds is a scheduled interval, not a guarantee that you have recovered. If you are not ready to continue, end the session and take the rest you need. Do not push through pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or loss of balance to keep to the clock.

The clock continues even when the camera cannot read you. A running timer or the absence of a camera warning does not mean that continuing is suitable.
messages.s_773541d436b31c3f8fb4bb9e99470daf586700:
Twelve planned cycles of thirty seconds of work and thirty seconds of recovery make twelve minutes, with six minutes of work. Your control and comfort take priority over completing that schedule.

Work at a pace you can control. Do not trade movement form for speed.

If your guard, return or balance starts to drift, slow down. If you cannot restore comfortable control, end the session. Do not push through pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or loss of balance. Camera feedback cannot confirm that continuing is suitable for you.

The thirty-thirty cycle is a suggested schedule, not a measurement of your readiness or a personal exercise prescription. Reduce the pace or stop early when needed. The timer describes the plan; finishing it is not a test you have to pass.

messages.s_23a8d8b0f59c9a45d0095475956ec013ac62e3: Distinguish forward, circular and side-kick paths on paper. Roundhouse, high kicks, spins, jumps, impact and partner work are outside this first-release practice; do not imitate them physically for demonstration.

messages.s_2b3f6e1e15a5da2c9e533aec176fe110a349d6: Distinguish knee preparation from teep extension: knee stays bent and lower leg folded. messages.s_2b48a7909a8048cb233e60414a9fb8735af90d: Finish the first three units separately first. messages.s_2cf92bb171533d7fed261f3619a2eb9e1d1f9f: In parallel preparation, the feet occupy separate tracks around a comfortable hip-width spacing and face forward without force.
